items.headline: Top biotech deals in June 2026
items.preview: June 2026 saw significant acquisitions in the biopharma sector, led by AbbVie and GSK.
items.article:
June was a busy month for the biopharma industry. AbbVie’s $10.9 billion takeover of Apogee was the most expensive acquisition of last month. Drug development in oncology and neurology was popular among dealmakers, with mRNA therapies and small molecules also licensed.

The biggest acquisition deal announced in June was by pharma giant AbbVie, which plans to buy Massachusetts-based Apogee Therapeutics. This acquisition will hand over Apogee’s zumilokibart for atopic dermatitis, asthma, and eosinophilic esophagitis to AbbVie. GSK also made headlines by purchasing Nuvalent for $10.6 billion to enhance its cancer drug pipeline. Why this matters: These acquisitions reflect a strategic focus on expanding therapeutic pipelines in high-demand areas such as oncology and neurology, indicating ongoing investment in innovative treatments.

items.headline: Roche drops two Huntington’s programmes from Ionis
items.preview: Roche discontinues two Huntington's disease programs due to ineffective results.
items.article:
Roche has discontinued two Huntington’s disease programmes after its Ionis-partnered drug tominersen failed to improve patients’ symptoms. The decisions eliminate two of Roche’s three clinical approaches to lowering the toxic huntingtin protein that drives the neurodegenerative disease.

Roche’s phase 2 GENERATION HD2 trial found that tominersen significantly reduced mutant huntingtin but had no meaningful effect on clinical outcomes compared to placebo after 16 months. Meanwhile, Roche has also stopped the phase 1 POINT-HD trial of RG6496 due to concerns raised in animal studies. Why this matters: The discontinuation of these programs highlights the challenges in developing effective treatments for Huntington’s disease, a condition currently lacking approved disease-modifying therapies.

items.headline: With first clinical data due next year, Scribe to test IPO market
items.preview: Scribe Therapeutics files for an IPO as it begins clinical testing of its gene silencing therapy.
items.article:
Scribe Therapeutics has entered the NASDAQ queue just before the July 4 holiday weekend, aiming to test the IPO market. The company has begun first-in-human testing of its lead program, STX-1150, in Australia among patients at risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).

The treatment utilizes Scribe’s Epigenetic Long-Term X-Repressor (ELXR) technology to suppress expression of PCSK9, with initial data expected in the first half of 2027. Why this matters: The successful IPO could provide Scribe with the necessary capital to advance its innovative gene silencing therapies, potentially transforming treatment approaches for cardiovascular diseases.

items.headline: KAIST Creates AI to Detect Early Cerebrovascular Disease Signs at Home
items.preview: KAIST researchers develop AI to monitor behavioral changes for early cerebrovascular disease detection.
items.article:
South Korean researchers have unveiled an AI system capable of detecting early signs of cerebrovascular disease by monitoring subtle behavioral changes in older adults at home. This technology utilizes contactless sensors to analyze daily activity patterns and environmental factors, providing insights before clinical symptoms emerge.

The AI model achieved 96.5% accuracy in identifying individuals at risk of stroke. It highlights the potential for early intervention through continuous monitoring of behavioral health markers. Why this matters: This innovative approach could shift healthcare from reactive to preventive, potentially reducing the incidence of cerebrovascular diseases through personalized risk assessment.

items.headline: Social learning dynamically shapes moral decision-making by biasing subjective valuation
items.preview: Study reveals how social influence affects moral decision-making through valuation bias.
items.article:
Observing immoral behavior increases one’s dishonesty through social influence and learning processes. This study tested different mechanistic hypotheses to account for moral contagion using model-based fMRI and a cheating game.

The findings indicate that participants’ valuation was dynamically biased by learning that others had cheated. The research provides insights into the neurocomputational mechanisms underlying how social influence modifies moral decisions. Why this matters: Understanding these mechanisms can inform strategies to mitigate dishonest behavior in social contexts, enhancing ethical decision-making.
